Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Revaluation Account — nature
questions.question: The Revaluation Account prepared at the time of reconstitution of a firm is also known as the:
options: B) Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
D) Profit and Loss Adjustment Account
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Profit and Loss Adjustment Account
Why: The Revaluation Account records the profit or loss arising from revaluing assets and reassessing liabilities when the firm is reconstituted. For this reason NCERT also calls it the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account. Its balance is transferred to the old partners in the old ratio.
Why not the others:
(A) The Realisation Account is prepared only on dissolution.
(B) The Appropriation Account divides each year's profit.
(C) There is no standard account by that name for this purpose.
Key point: Reconstitution → Revaluation (P&L Adjustment) Account; dissolution → Realisation Account.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account — profit or loss with assets taken over
questions.question: On dissolution: assets other than cash were ₹2,00,000 (including investments of ₹20,000); creditors were ₹50,000; and bills payable were ₹10,000. Partner A took over the investments at ₹18,000, and the other assets realised ₹1,70,000. Creditors accepted ₹48,000 in full settlement; bills payable were paid in full; and realisation expenses were ₹3,000. The loss on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹13,000
Step 1: Debit side = Assets ₹2,00,000 + Creditors paid ₹48,000 + Bills payable paid ₹10,000 + Expenses ₹3,000 = ₹2,61,000
Step 2: Credit side = Creditors ₹50,000 + Bills payable ₹10,000 + Cash from assets ₹1,70,000 + Investments taken by A ₹18,000 = ₹2,48,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹2,61,000 − ₹2,48,000 = ₹13,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the ₹2,000 discount from creditors gives ₹15,000 (A). Valuing the investments taken over at book value (₹20,000) gives ₹11,000 (C). Ignoring the expenses gives ₹10,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — finding the opening capital
questions.question: Partners' capitals are fluctuating. A's capital on 31 March 2026 is ₹1,50,000. During the year: his drawings were ₹30,000; his share of profit of ₹40,000 was credited; and he introduced additional capital of ₹20,000. Interest on capital is allowed at 10% p.a. on the OPENING capital only. The interest on A's capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹12,000
Why: Work backwards from the closing capital — add back what reduced it, and deduct what increased it.
Step 1: Opening capital = Closing ₹1,50,000 + Drawings ₹30,000 − Share of profit ₹40,000 − Additional capital ₹20,000 = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Interest = 10% × ₹1,20,000 = ₹12,000
Common mistake: Calculating interest on the closing capital gives ₹15,000 (A). Forgetting to deduct the additional capital (opening ₹1,40,000) gives ₹14,000 (C). Adding back the drawings but ignoring both the profit and the additional capital (₹1,80,000) gives ₹18,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription and minimum subscription
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the issue of shares:
(A) In case of over-subscription, the company may reject some applications and refund their money.
(B) The excess application money of applicants allotted shares pro-rata may be adjusted towards the allotment money.
(C) Excess application money may be refunded to the applicants.
(D) Shares may be allotted even if the minimum subscription has not been received.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: On over-subscription the directors may reject some applications outright (A), allot pro-rata and adjust the excess money towards allotment and calls (B), or refund the excess (C). These are the three ways of dealing with over-subscription that NCERT describes.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — under Section 39 of the Companies Act, 2013 no allotment can be made unless the minimum subscription is received. Options (A), (B) and (C) all include (D).
Key point: Over-subscription → reject / pro-rata / refund; below minimum subscription → no allotment.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — profit distributed in the wrong ratio
questions.question: A, B and C should have shared profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1, but the profit of ₹60,000 for the year was wrongly distributed equally. Their capitals are fixed. The single adjusting entry is:
options: A) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To C's Current A/c ₹10,000
B) C's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To A's and B's Current A/cs ₹5,000 each
C) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To A's Current A/c ₹10,000
D) C's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To A's Current A/c ₹10,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To A's Current A/c ₹10,000
Step 1: Correct shares (3 : 2 : 1): A ₹30,000; B ₹20,000; C ₹10,000
Step 2: Shares actually credited: ₹20,000 each
Step 3: Difference: A +₹10,000 (short-credited); B nil; C −₹10,000 (excess)
Step 4: Entry: C's Current A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To A's Current A/c ₹10,000
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (A). Spreading C's excess over A and B gives (B), but B was already correctly paid. (C) debits B, who needs no adjustment.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit to the firm by a partner
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. B has guaranteed that the firm's profit will not be less than ₹1,00,000, and he will make good any shortfall personally. The actual profit for the year is ₹84,000. B's final share of profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹24,000
Given: The guarantee is given to the FIRM (not to a partner); guaranteed profit ₹1,00,000; actual ₹84,000; B bears the shortfall.
Step 1: Shortfall = ₹1,00,000 − ₹84,000 = ₹16,000, borne by B
Step 2: The firm distributes the guaranteed ₹1,00,000 in 3 : 2 → A ₹60,000; B ₹40,000
Step 3: B's net share = ₹40,000 − ₹16,000 = ₹24,000 (A gets ₹60,000; total ₹84,000 ✔)
Common mistake: Ignoring the guarantee gives B ₹33,600 (A). Forgetting to charge B the shortfall gives ₹40,000 (B). Deducting the shortfall from B's share of ₹84,000 gives ₹17,600 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — types of shares
questions.question: Shares issued by a company to its employees or directors at a discount, or for consideration other than cash, for providing know-how or making available rights in the nature of intellectual property, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Sweat equity shares
Why: Section 54 of the Companies Act, 2013 permits sweat equity shares as a reward for the know-how or value-adding efforts ('sweat') of employees and directors. They are the only shares a company may issue at a discount.
Why not the others:
(B) Bonus shares are issued free to existing shareholders out of reserves.
(C) Right shares are offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holding.
(D) Preference shares carry preferential rights to dividend and capital.
Key point: Sweat equity = the exception to the 'no discount on shares' rule (Section 53).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — adjustment of goodwill
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 4 : 3 : 3. They decide to share future profits in the ratio 1 : 2 : 2. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. In the single adjusting entry for goodwill, the amount credited to A's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹30,000
Given: Old ratio 4/10, 3/10, 3/10; new ratio 2/10, 4/10, 4/10; goodwill ₹1,50,000.
Step 1: A = 4/10 − 2/10 = 2/10 sacrifice; B = 3/10 − 4/10 = 1/10 gain; C = 3/10 − 4/10 = 1/10 gain
Step 2: A is compensated for 2/10 of goodwill = ₹30,000, paid ₹15,000 each by B and C
Step 3: Entry: B's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹30,000
Common mistake: ₹15,000 (A) is what each gaining partner pays. ₹60,000 (C) is A's old share of the total goodwill. ₹45,000 (D) is B's old share of the total goodwill.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Salary to a partner — appropriation
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Salary payable to a partner under the partnership deed is shown in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
Reason (R): Salary to a partner is an appropriation of profit and not a charge against profit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: A partner is an owner, not an employee. Salary to him is a way of distributing profit, so it is debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and allowed only out of profits. Because it is an appropriation (the Reason), it appears in the Appropriation Account (the Assertion).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains why the Assertion is true. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Salary to an employee → P&L Account (charge); salary to a partner → P&L Appropriation Account.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Loan by a partner's relative on dissolution
questions.question: On dissolution, a loan given to the firm by a partner's wife is:
options: A) Transferred to the partner's Capital Account
B) Paid after the partners' capitals are repaid
C) Transferred to the Realisation Account and paid along with the other outside liabilities
D) Paid only if there is a profit on realisation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Transferred to the Realisation Account and paid along with the other outside liabilities
Why: A partner's wife is a third party (an outsider), not a partner. Her loan is an outside liability, so it is transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account and paid first, under Section 48(b)(i).
Why not the others:
(A) The firm owes her, not the partner.
(B) Capital is repaid last; outsiders come first.
(D) Outside debts are payable whether or not there is a realisation profit.
Key point: Loan by a partner → Partner's Loan A/c (paid after outsiders); loan by a partner's relative → outside liability.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — new ratio when the share is taken from one partner
questions.question: Partners A and B share profits 3 : 1. B does not want to give up any part of his share, so C, who joins for a 1/5th share, acquires it wholly from A. What is the profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C after C's admission?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 11 : 5 : 4
Step 1: A's new share = 3/4 − 1/5 = 15/20 − 4/20 = 11/20
Step 2: B's share is unchanged = 1/4 = 5/20
Step 3: C's share = 1/5 = 4/20
Step 4: New ratio = 11 : 5 : 4
Common mistake: If C took his share from A and B in their old ratio, the result would be 12 : 4 : 4 = 3 : 1 : 1 (A). Taking C's share entirely from B gives 15 : 1 : 4 (B). (C) swaps B's and C's shares.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — accounting treatment as per AS-26
questions.question: As per AS-26 (Intangible Assets), goodwill that is internally generated by a firm:
options: A) Is not recognised as an asset in the books
B) Is recorded at the cost of building it
C) Is recorded at its current market value
D) Is shown as a current asset
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Is not recognised as an asset in the books
Why: AS-26 allows only PURCHASED goodwill (goodwill for which consideration has been paid) to be recorded. Internally generated goodwill cannot be measured reliably at cost. This is why, at admission or retirement, goodwill is adjusted through partners' capital accounts instead of being raised in the books.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) record a value that AS-26 does not allow. (D) Goodwill is never a current asset.
Key point: Purchased goodwill → recorded; self-generated goodwill → not recorded.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — adjustment of old partners' capitals
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 2 : 1, and their capitals after all adjustments are ₹1,30,000 and ₹50,000. C is admitted for a 1/4th share and brings ₹60,000 as capital. The old partners' capitals are to be adjusted on the basis of C's capital, in their profit-sharing ratio, by bringing in or withdrawing cash. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A withdraws ₹10,000; B brings ₹10,000
Step 1: Total capital of the new firm = ₹60,000 × 4/1 = ₹2,40,000
Step 2: Old partners' combined share (3/4) = ₹1,80,000, divided in their ratio 2 : 1 → A ₹1,20,000; B ₹60,000
Step 3: A has ₹1,30,000 → excess ₹10,000 withdrawn; B has ₹50,000 → shortage ₹10,000 brought in
Common mistake: Reversing the adjustments gives (A). Assuming both have excess gives (B). Measuring each partner's difference from ₹1,50,000 (an equal split) gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Fixed versus fluctuating capital
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Under the fixed capital method, a partner's Capital Account normally shows the same credit balance year after year unless capital is added or withdrawn.
(B) Under the fluctuating capital method, two accounts are maintained for each partner.
(C) Under the fixed capital method, a partner's Current Account may show a debit balance.
(D) Under the fixed capital method, drawings are debited to the Current Account.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why:
(A) True — only permanent changes in capital affect the Capital Account.
(C) True — if drawings and losses exceed the credits, the Current Account turns debit.
(D) True — all routine items, including drawings, go to the Current Account.
(B) False — the fluctuating capital method has only ONE account (the Capital Account) per partner; two accounts are a feature of the fixed capital method.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (B).
Key point: Fixed → Capital A/c + Current A/c; fluctuating → Capital A/c only.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — existing goodwill and goodwill adjustment
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. Goodwill appears in their books at ₹30,000. C retires, and the firm's goodwill is valued at ₹60,000. A and B continue to share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. The existing goodwill is written off. The total amount debited to A's Capital Account in respect of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹21,000
Step 1: Write off the existing goodwill among ALL old partners in the old ratio: A's share = ₹30,000 × 3/6 = ₹15,000 (debit)
Step 2: C's share of the new goodwill = ₹60,000 × 1/6 = ₹10,000
Step 3: Gaining ratio: A = 3/5 − 3/6 = 3/30; B = 2/5 − 2/6 = 2/30 → 3 : 2, so A bears ₹10,000 × 3/5 = ₹6,000 (debit)
Step 4: Total debit to A = ₹15,000 + ₹6,000 = ₹21,000
Common mistake: Taking only the write-off gives ₹15,000 (A). Taking only the goodwill adjustment gives ₹6,000 (B). ₹30,000 (D) is A's share of the new goodwill, which is never raised under AS-26.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — quarterly drawings
questions.question: Raman, a partner, draws ₹15,000 on the first day of every quarter (1 April, 1 July, 1 October and 1 January) for his personal use. The firm closes its books on 31 March 2026 and charges interest on drawings at 10% p.a. How much interest will be charged on Raman's drawings for the year?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹3,750
Given: 4 drawings of ₹15,000 = ₹60,000, at the beginning of each quarter; rate 10% p.a.
Formula: For drawings at the beginning of each quarter, average period = (12 + 3) ÷ 2 = 7.5 months
Step 1: Interest = ₹60,000 × 10% × 7.5/12 = ₹3,750
Check: 15,000 × 10% × (12 + 9 + 6 + 3)/12 = ₹3,750 ✔
Common mistake: Drawings at the END of each quarter (average 4.5 months) give ₹2,250 (A). Using 6 months gives ₹3,000 (B). Charging the full year gives ₹6,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation Account — credit side
questions.question: Which of the following is credited to the Realisation Account?
options: A) Assets (other than cash) at book value
B) Realisation expenses paid by the firm
D) Outside liabilities transferred at book value
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Outside liabilities transferred at book value
Why: The Realisation Account is debited with assets and payments, and credited with liabilities and receipts. Outside liabilities (creditors, bills payable, loans) are transferred to its credit side when the firm is dissolved.
Why not the others:
(A) Assets are transferred to the DEBIT side.
(B) Expenses are debited.
(C) Payments of liabilities are debited (Realisation A/c Dr.; To Cash).
Key point: Debit = assets + payments; credit = liabilities + cash received.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — weighted average profit method
questions.question: A firm's profits were: 2022-23 ₹50,000; 2023-24 ₹60,000; 2024-25 ₹80,000. Weights of 1, 2 and 3 are assigned to these years respectively. Goodwill is valued at two years' purchase of the weighted average profit. The value of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,36,667
Formula: Weighted average profit = Σ(Profit × Weight) ÷ Σ Weights
Step 1: Products: 50,000 × 1 = 50,000; 60,000 × 2 = 1,20,000; 80,000 × 3 = 2,40,000; total ₹4,10,000
Step 2: Weighted average = ₹4,10,000 ÷ 6 = ₹68,333 (approx.)
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹68,333.33 × 2 = ₹1,36,667 (approx.)
Common mistake: Using the simple average (₹63,333) gives ₹1,26,667 (A). ₹68,333 (B) is the weighted average itself. Taking only the latest year gives ₹1,60,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Over-subscription — cash received on allotment
questions.question: A company offered 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, payable ₹3 on application and ₹4 on allotment (the balance later). Applications were received for 1,50,000 shares. Applications for 30,000 shares were rejected and the money refunded, and the remaining applicants were allotted shares on a pro-rata basis, with their excess application money adjusted towards allotment. All allotment money due was received. The cash received on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹3,40,000
Step 1: Pro-rata applicants applied for 1,50,000 − 30,000 = 1,20,000 shares and got 1,00,000
Step 2: Excess application money = 20,000 × ₹3 = ₹60,000, adjusted towards allotment
Step 3: Allotment due = 1,00,000 × ₹4 = ₹4,00,000
Step 4: Cash received = ₹4,00,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹3,40,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the adjustment gives ₹4,00,000 (B). Adjusting on the 30,000 rejected shares instead gives ₹3,10,000 (C). Adjusting on all 50,000 excess shares gives ₹2,50,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — sharing of revaluation profit
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Profit on revaluation at the time of admission is shared by all the partners, including the new partner, in the new profit-sharing ratio.
Reason (R): Changes in the values of assets and liabilities relate to the period before the admission of the new partner.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: The rise or fall in asset values took place while only the old partners owned the firm (the Reason is true). So the revaluation profit belongs to the OLD partners only, in their OLD ratio — the new partner gets no share, and the Assertion is false.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) treat the Assertion as true.
Key point: Anything earned or lost before admission (revaluation, reserves, accumulated profits) → old partners, old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Calls in advance received with allotment
questions.question: A company allotted 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, with ₹4 per share payable on allotment. A shareholder holding 500 shares also paid the first call of ₹3 per share along with the allotment money. The total cash received at the time of allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹41,500
Step 1: Allotment money on all shares = 10,000 × ₹4 = ₹40,000
Step 2: Calls in advance = 500 × ₹3 = ₹1,500 (credited to Calls in Advance A/c, a liability, until the call is made)
Step 3: Cash received = ₹40,000 + ₹1,500 = ₹41,500
Common mistake: Ignoring the advance gives ₹40,000 (B). Assuming the advance was ₹3,000 gives ₹43,000 (C). Deducting the advance instead of adding it gives ₹38,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death of a partner — executor's account paid in instalments
questions.question: The amount due to a deceased partner's executor is ₹1,20,000. It is agreed to pay this in three equal annual instalments of principal, with interest at 10% p.a. on the outstanding balance. The total amount paid at the end of the first year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹52,000
Step 1: Principal instalment = ₹1,20,000 ÷ 3 = ₹40,000
Step 2: Interest for year 1 = 10% × ₹1,20,000 (balance outstanding during year 1) = ₹12,000
Step 3: Total payment = ₹40,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹52,000 (the Executor's Loan A/c is credited with interest and debited with payment)
Common mistake: Paying only the principal gives ₹40,000 (A). Charging interest only on the instalment gives ₹44,000 (C). ₹48,254 (D) is an equal total instalment (annuity), which was not agreed here.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — gaining ratio when the new ratio is given
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. C retires, and A and B decide to share future profits in the ratio 2 : 1. Their gaining ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5 : 1
Formula: Gain = New share − Old share
Step 1: A = 2/3 − 5/10 = 20/30 − 15/30 = 5/30
Step 2: B = 1/3 − 3/10 = 10/30 − 9/30 = 1/30
Step 3: Gaining ratio = 5 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming the new ratio is the gaining ratio gives 2 : 1 (B). That holds only when the retiring partner's share is taken in the new ratio. 5 : 3 (C) is the old ratio of A and B. 1 : 1 (D) assumes equal gains.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Division of profit — salary and commission to partners
questions.question: The profit of a firm before partners' salary and commission is ₹2,60,000. Partner A is entitled to a salary of ₹5,000 per month. Partner B is entitled to a commission of 5% of the net profit after charging A's salary but before charging his own commission. The profit available for distribution in the profit-sharing ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,90,000
Step 1: A's salary = ₹5,000 × 12 = ₹60,000
Step 2: Profit after salary = ₹2,60,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹2,00,000
Step 3: B's commission = 5% × ₹2,00,000 = ₹10,000 (before charging the commission, so no 5/105 adjustment)
Step 4: Divisible profit = ₹2,00,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹1,90,000
Common mistake: Forgetting the commission gives ₹2,00,000 (B). Calculating the commission on ₹2,60,000 gives ₹1,87,000 (C). Applying the 'after charging commission' formula (5/105) gives ₹1,90,476 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — capitalisation of super profit method
questions.question: A firm's average profit is ₹90,000 and its capital employed is ₹6,00,000. The normal rate of return is 12%. The value of goodwill by capitalising the super profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,50,000
Formula: Goodwill = Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return
Step 1: Normal profit = ₹6,00,000 × 12% = ₹72,000
Step 2: Super profit = ₹90,000 − ₹72,000 = ₹18,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹18,000 × 100/12 = ₹1,50,000
Check: Capitalised value of average profit ₹7,50,000 − capital employed ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,50,000 ✔ (both capitalisation methods give the same answer)
Common mistake: ₹7,50,000 (A) is the capitalised value of average profit before deducting capital employed. Using two years' purchase of super profit gives ₹36,000 (C). ₹18,000 (D) is the super profit itself.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Steps in settlement of accounts on dissolution
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps in the settlement of accounts on dissolution of a firm in the correct order:
(A) Transfer assets (other than cash and bank) and outside liabilities to the Realisation Account
(B) Record the sale of assets and the payment of liabilities
(C) Transfer the profit or loss on realisation to the partners' capital accounts
(D) Settle the partners' capital accounts through the Cash/Bank Account
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B), (C), (D)
Why: Each step needs the one before it.
1. Assets and outside liabilities are first closed into the Realisation Account (A).
2. Their sale and settlement are then recorded (B).
3. Only after all items are settled is the profit or loss on realisation known and transferred to the partners (C).
4. The capital accounts, now complete, are closed by paying or receiving cash (D).
Why not the others: (B) records sales before transferring the assets; (C) finds the profit before the sales; (D) closes the capitals before sharing the realisation result.
Key point: Transfer → realise → share the result → settle.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Partnership deed — meaning
questions.question: A partnership deed is best described as:
options: A) The certificate of registration issued by the Registrar of Firms
B) A written agreement among the partners containing the terms of the partnership
C) A document needed only for opening the firm's bank account
D) The balance sheet prepared at the end of the first year
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A written agreement among the partners containing the terms of the partnership
Why: The deed records matters such as capital contribution, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and drawings, salaries and the rules for admission and retirement. It prevents disputes, and it is signed by the partners and stamped as per the Stamp Act.
Why not the others:
(A) A registration certificate is issued by the Registrar, while the deed is made by the partners.
(C) A bank may ask for it, but that is not its purpose.
(D) The balance sheet is a financial statement, not an agreement.
Key point: Deed = written terms; if there is no deed, the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 applies.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Change in profit-sharing ratio — reserves not distributed
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. They decide to share profits equally in future. The balance sheet shows a General Reserve of ₹40,000, which the partners do NOT want to distribute. The adjusting entry is:
options: A) A's Capital A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹4,000
B) General Reserve A/c Dr. ₹40,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹24,000 and B's Capital A/c ₹16,000
C) B's Capital A/c Dr. ₹8,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹8,000
D) B's Capital A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹4,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) B's Capital A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹4,000
Given: Old ratio 3 : 2; new ratio 1 : 1; reserve ₹40,000 to remain in the books.
Step 1: A: 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10 sacrifice; B: 2/5 − 1/2 = −1/10 gain
Step 2: Adjustment = ₹40,000 × 1/10 = ₹4,000
Step 3: The gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner: B's Capital A/c Dr. ₹4,000; To A's Capital A/c ₹4,000
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (A). (B) distributes the reserve, which the partners did not want. Using the change in A's share as 2/10 gives ₹8,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Presentation of share capital — subscribed capital with forfeiture
questions.question: A company has authorised capital of 1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It issued 80,000 shares, of which 75,000 were subscribed. ₹8 per share has been called up. Calls in arrears are ₹6,000. 500 shares, on which ₹6 per share had been received, were forfeited and have not yet been re-issued. The total amount shown under 'Share Capital' in the balance sheet (including the forfeited shares) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹5,93,000
Step 1: Shares outstanding after forfeiture = 75,000 − 500 = 74,500; called up 74,500 × ₹8 = ₹5,96,000
Step 2: Less calls in arrears = ₹6,000 → ₹5,90,000
Step 3: Add forfeited shares (amount received on them) = 500 × ₹6 = ₹3,000
Step 4: Share Capital = ₹5,90,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹5,93,000
Common mistake: 75,000 × ₹8 = ₹6,00,000 (A) ignores both the forfeiture and the arrears. Leaving out the forfeited amount gives ₹5,90,000 (C). Ignoring the calls in arrears gives ₹5,99,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — treatment of goodwill (AS-26)
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the treatment of goodwill on the admission of a partner:
(A) Under AS-26, goodwill is not raised in the books at the time of admission.
(B) Premium for goodwill brought in cash is credited to the sacrificing partners in their sacrificing ratio.
(C) If the new partner does not bring his share of goodwill in cash, his Capital Account is credited with that amount.
(D) The old partners may withdraw the premium brought in by the new partner.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why:
(A) True — internally generated goodwill cannot be recognised.
(B) True — premium compensates the partners who give up their share.
(D) True — the premium may be retained in the business or withdrawn, and a withdrawal is recorded through the partners' capital accounts.
(C) False — if the premium is not brought in cash, the new partner's Capital (or Current) Account is DEBITED with his share of goodwill and the sacrificing partners are credited.
Why not the others: Options (B), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (C).
Key point: Premium not brought in → debit the new partner, credit the sacrificing partners.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares at a premium — instalments
questions.question: A company issued 5,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹3 per share, payable as: ₹4 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including the premium) and ₹4 on the first and final call. The amount credited to the Share Capital Account on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹10,000
Step 1: Allotment money ₹5 per share = ₹2 towards capital + ₹3 premium
Step 2: Share Capital credit = 5,000 × ₹2 = ₹10,000; Securities Premium credit = 5,000 × ₹3 = ₹15,000
Entry: Share Allotment A/c Dr. ₹25,000; To Share Capital A/c ₹10,000; To Securities Premium A/c ₹15,000
Common mistake: Crediting the whole allotment to capital gives ₹25,000 (A). ₹15,000 (B) is the premium. ₹20,000 (D) is the capital part of the application money.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture of shares
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the forfeiture of shares:
(A) Forfeiture means cancellation of shares for non-payment of allotment or call money.
(B) On forfeiture, the Share Capital Account is debited with the amount called up on those shares.
(C) Securities Premium already received on the forfeited shares is debited on forfeiture.
(D) Until re-issue, the balance in the Share Forfeiture Account is added to paid-up capital in the notes to Share Capital.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why:
(A) True — this is the definition, done as per the Articles (Table F).
(B) True — the called-up amount is reversed from Share Capital.
(D) True — Schedule III requires the forfeited amount to be added to paid-up capital until the shares are re-issued.
(C) False — premium that has been RECEIVED is never cancelled. Securities Premium is debited only if the premium was due but NOT received.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (C).
Key point: Premium received stays; premium unpaid is reversed on forfeiture.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — methods of valuation
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Method of valuing goodwill)
(A) Average profit method
(B) Super profit method
(C) Capitalisation of average profit method
(D) Capitalisation of super profit method

List-II (Formula)
(I) Super profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return
(II) Average profit × Number of years' purchase
(III) Super profit × Number of years' purchase
(IV) (Average profit × 100 ÷ Normal rate of return) − Capital employed

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) Average profit method: average profit × years' purchase → (II).
(B) Super profit method: super profit × years' purchase → (III).
(C) Capitalisation of average profit: capitalised value of average profit less capital employed → (IV).
(D) Capitalisation of super profit: super profit capitalised at the normal rate → (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two methods; (B) swaps the two capitalisation methods; (D) swaps the super profit methods.
Key point: 'Years' purchase' → multiply; 'capitalisation' → × 100 ÷ normal rate.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation of debtors with a provision
questions.question: On dissolution, debtors of ₹50,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of ₹4,000 were transferred to the Realisation Account. The debtors realised ₹43,000. The loss on realisation of debtors is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹3,000
Why: Debtors are transferred at their GROSS value (debit) and the provision is transferred to the credit side of the Realisation Account.
Step 1: Debit: Debtors ₹50,000
Step 2: Credit: Provision ₹4,000 + Cash realised ₹43,000 = ₹47,000
Step 3: Loss = ₹50,000 − ₹47,000 = ₹3,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the provision gives ₹7,000 (A). ₹4,000 (C) is the provision itself. Taking the provision minus the loss gives ₹1,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Features and types of companies
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II with reference to the Companies Act, 2013:

List-I (Type of company)
(A) Private company
(B) Public company
(C) One Person Company
(D) Government company

List-II (Feature)
(I) Minimum seven members
(II) Maximum two hundred members
(III) Only one member
(IV) At least 51% of the paid-up share capital held by the government

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) A private company may have at most 200 members (Section 2(68)) → (II).
(B) A public company needs at least 7 members, with no upper limit → (I).
(C) A One Person Company has a single member (Section 2(62)) → (III).
(D) A government company has at least 51% of its paid-up capital held by the Central and/or State Government (Section 2(45)) → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps private and public companies; (B) and (C) misplace the One Person Company.
Key point: Private ≤ 200; public ≥ 7; OPC = 1; government ≥ 51%.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of debentures at a discount — amount received
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

On 1 July 2025, Sunrise Ltd. issued 4,000, 10% debentures of ₹500 each at a discount of 4%, redeemable at a premium of 6% after five years. Interest is payable half-yearly on 31 December and 30 June. On 31 March 2026, the end of its financial year, the company's Securities Premium Account had a balance of ₹30,000. The company decided to use this balance first for writing off the loss on issue of debentures (as permitted by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013), and to write off the remaining loss to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the same year.

Question: The amount received by the company on the issue of debentures is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹19,20,000
Step 1: Issue price = ₹500 − 4% discount (₹20) = ₹480
Step 2: Amount received = 4,000 × ₹480 = ₹19,20,000
Common mistake: ₹20,00,000 (A) is the face value. Adding the redemption premium gives ₹21,20,000 (C), which is the amount payable on redemption. Adding the discount instead of deducting it gives ₹20,80,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Loss on issue of debentures
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

On 1 July 2025, Sunrise Ltd. issued 4,000, 10% debentures of ₹500 each at a discount of 4%, redeemable at a premium of 6% after five years. Interest is payable half-yearly on 31 December and 30 June. On 31 March 2026, the end of its financial year, the company's Securities Premium Account had a balance of ₹30,000. The company decided to use this balance first for writing off the loss on issue of debentures (as permitted by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013), and to write off the remaining loss to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the same year.

Question: The total loss on issue of debentures is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹2,00,000
Formula: Loss on issue = Discount on issue + Premium on redemption
Step 1: Discount = 4,000 × ₹20 = ₹80,000
Step 2: Premium on redemption = 4,000 × ₹30 (6% of ₹500) = ₹1,20,000
Step 3: Loss on issue = ₹80,000 + ₹1,20,000 = ₹2,00,000
Common mistake: ₹80,000 (A) counts only the discount. ₹1,20,000 (C) counts only the redemption premium. Netting the two percentages (6% − 4% = 2%) gives ₹40,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Premium on redemption of debentures — presentation
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

On 1 July 2025, Sunrise Ltd. issued 4,000, 10% debentures of ₹500 each at a discount of 4%, redeemable at a premium of 6% after five years. Interest is payable half-yearly on 31 December and 30 June. On 31 March 2026, the end of its financial year, the company's Securities Premium Account had a balance of ₹30,000. The company decided to use this balance first for writing off the loss on issue of debentures (as permitted by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013), and to write off the remaining loss to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the same year.

Question: In the balance sheet of Sunrise Ltd. as at 31 March 2026, the Premium on Redemption of Debentures Account will be shown under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Other long-term liabilities
Why: The ₹1,20,000 premium is an amount the company must PAY to debenture holders on redemption after five years. So it is a non-current liability, shown under 'Other long-term liabilities' (it becomes current only in the year of redemption).
Why not the others:
(A) It is not a reserve — it is owed to outsiders.
(B) Provisions are estimated liabilities; this amount is fixed.
(C) Long-term borrowings show the debentures themselves (₹20,00,000), not the premium.
Key point: Debentures → long-term borrowings; redemption premium → other long-term liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Interest on debentures — accrued interest
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

On 1 July 2025, Sunrise Ltd. issued 4,000, 10% debentures of ₹500 each at a discount of 4%, redeemable at a premium of 6% after five years. Interest is payable half-yearly on 31 December and 30 June. On 31 March 2026, the end of its financial year, the company's Securities Premium Account had a balance of ₹30,000. The company decided to use this balance first for writing off the loss on issue of debentures (as permitted by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013), and to write off the remaining loss to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the same year.

Question: The interest on debentures accrued but not due on 31 March 2026 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹50,000
Given: Interest is always on the FACE value (₹20,00,000) at 10% p.a.
Step 1: Interest paid on 31 December 2025 (July–December, 6 months) = ₹20,00,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Interest for January–March 2026 (3 months) = ₹20,00,000 × 10% × 3/12 = ₹50,000. It is not payable until 30 June, so it is accrued but not due (shown under Other current liabilities).
Common mistake: ₹1,00,000 (A) is the half-yearly amount already paid. ₹1,50,000 (B) is the total interest for the year. Calculating on the issue price of ₹19,20,000 gives ₹48,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Writing off loss on issue and finance cost for the year
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

On 1 July 2025, Sunrise Ltd. issued 4,000, 10% debentures of ₹500 each at a discount of 4%, redeemable at a premium of 6% after five years. Interest is payable half-yearly on 31 December and 30 June. On 31 March 2026, the end of its financial year, the company's Securities Premium Account had a balance of ₹30,000. The company decided to use this balance first for writing off the loss on issue of debentures (as permitted by Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013), and to write off the remaining loss to the Statement of Profit and Loss in the same year.

Question: The total amount charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss for 2025-26 in respect of these debentures (interest plus the loss on issue written off) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹3,20,000
Step 1: Interest for 9 months (1 July 2025 to 31 March 2026) = ₹20,00,000 × 10% × 9/12 = ₹1,50,000
Step 2: Loss on issue ₹2,00,000; less Securities Premium used ₹30,000 = ₹1,70,000 written off to P&L
Step 3: Total charged = ₹1,50,000 + ₹1,70,000 = ₹3,20,000
Common mistake: Not using the Securities Premium gives ₹3,50,000 (B). Leaving out the interest gives ₹1,70,000 (C). Charging a full year's interest (₹2,00,000) gives ₹3,70,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — cash and cash equivalents
questions.question:
As per AS-3 (Revised), which of the following are 'cash and cash equivalents'?
(A) Cash in hand
(B) Demand deposits with banks
(C) Short-term, highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less
(D) Equity shares held as current investments
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Cash means cash in hand and demand deposits (A, B). Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with an insignificant risk of change in value — usually with a maturity of three months or less (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — equity shares carry a significant risk of change in value, so AS-3 excludes them from cash equivalents. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Cash equivalent = short maturity + no significant value risk.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — net profit ratio
questions.question: Revenue from operations is ₹6,00,000. Net profit before tax is ₹90,000 and the tax rate is 30%. The net profit ratio, based on profit after tax, is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 10.5%
Step 1: Tax = 30% × ₹90,000 = ₹27,000; net profit after tax = ₹63,000
Step 2: Net profit ratio = ₹63,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 × 100 = 10.5%
Common mistake: Using profit before tax gives 15% (B). ₹27,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 4.5% (C) is the tax as a percentage of revenue. Deducting tax twice gives 9% (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — Schedule III headings
questions.question: Which of the following items is shown under 'Other current liabilities' in a company's balance sheet prepared as per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Unpaid dividend
Why: Dividend that has been declared but not yet claimed or paid is a definite amount owed to shareholders, payable within 12 months. Schedule III therefore places it under Other current liabilities (along with calls in advance and interest accrued on borrowings).
Why not the others:
(B) Provision for tax is an estimated liability, shown under Short-term provisions.
(C) Bills payable are shown under Trade payables.
(D) Securities premium is shown under Reserves and Surplus in shareholders' funds.
Key point: Definite, non-trade amounts due within a year → Other current liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Liquidity ratios — current ratio from items
questions.question: From the following information, calculate the current ratio: Inventory ₹50,000; Trade receivables ₹70,000; Cash ₹20,000; Prepaid expenses ₹10,000; Trade payables ₹60,000; Outstanding expenses ₹15,000.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2 : 1
Step 1: Current assets = 50,000 + 70,000 + 20,000 + 10,000 = ₹1,50,000
Step 2: Current liabilities = 60,000 + 15,000 = ₹75,000
Step 3: Current ratio = ₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹75,000 = 2 : 1
Common mistake: Leaving out prepaid expenses gives 1.87 : 1 (A); prepaid expenses ARE current assets — they are excluded only from quick assets. Leaving out outstanding expenses gives 2.5 : 1 (B). 1.2 : 1 (C) is the quick ratio.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — net profit before tax (adjustments for dividend and tax)
questions.question: The balance in the Statement of Profit and Loss (Surplus) increased from ₹50,000 to ₹1,30,000 during the year. During the year: dividend of ₹30,000 for the previous year was paid; ₹20,000 was transferred to General Reserve; and a provision for tax of ₹40,000 was made. For the cash flow statement, the net profit before tax is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹1,70,000
Why: The increase in Surplus is profit AFTER the appropriations made from it. Add back each appropriation to reach net profit before tax.
Step 1: Increase in Surplus = ₹1,30,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹80,000
Step 2: Add the dividend paid out of Surplus = +₹30,000
Step 3: Add the transfer to General Reserve = +₹20,000
Step 4: Add the provision for tax = +₹40,000
Step 5: Net profit before tax = ₹1,70,000
Common mistake: ₹80,000 (A) is only the change in Surplus. Leaving out the tax gives ₹1,30,000 (B). Leaving out the reserve transfer gives ₹1,50,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Accounting ratios — formulas
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Ratio)
(A) Total assets to debt ratio
(B) Return on investment
(C) Operating ratio
(D) Trade receivables turnover ratio

List-II (Formula)
(I) (Cost of revenue from operations + Operating expenses) ÷ Revenue from operations × 100
(II) Total assets ÷ Long-term debts
(III) Net profit before interest and tax ÷ Capital employed × 100
(IV) Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Total assets to debt = Total assets ÷ Long-term debts (a solvency ratio) → (II).
(B) ROI = PBIT ÷ Capital employed × 100 → (III).
(C) Operating ratio = (Cost of revenue + Operating expenses) ÷ Revenue × 100; operating ratio + operating profit ratio = 100% → (I).
(D) Trade receivables turnover = Credit revenue ÷ Average trade receivables → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps total-assets-to-debt and ROI; (B) swaps ROI and operating ratio; (C) swaps the operating ratio and receivables turnover.
Key point: Learn the numerator and the denominator of each ratio together.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — return on investment
questions.question: A company has: Equity share capital ₹5,00,000; Reserves and surplus ₹2,00,000; 10% Debentures ₹3,00,000. Its net profit after interest and tax is ₹1,05,000, and the tax rate is 30%. Its return on investment (ROI) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 18%
Step 1: Capital employed = 5,00,000 + 2,00,000 + 3,00,000 = ₹10,00,000
Step 2: Profit before tax = ₹1,05,000 ÷ 0.70 = ₹1,50,000
Step 3: Interest on debentures = 10% × ₹3,00,000 = ₹30,000 → PBIT = ₹1,80,000
Step 4: ROI = ₹1,80,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 × 100 = 18%
Common mistake: Using profit before tax gives 15% (B). Using profit after tax gives 10.5% (C). Dividing PBIT by shareholders' funds only (₹7,00,000) gives 25.7% (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — trade payables turnover
questions.question: Net credit purchases are ₹4,80,000. At the beginning of the year, creditors were ₹40,000 and bills payable ₹10,000. At the end of the year, creditors were ₹55,000 and bills payable ₹15,000. The trade payables turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 8 times
Formula: Trade payables turnover = Net credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables (creditors + bills payable)
Step 1: Opening trade payables = ₹50,000; closing = ₹70,000
Step 2: Average = (₹50,000 + ₹70,000) ÷ 2 = ₹60,000
Step 3: Ratio = ₹4,80,000 ÷ ₹60,000 = 8 times
Common mistake: Leaving out bills payable (average ₹47,500) gives 10.1 times (A). Using the closing balance gives 6.86 times (C). Using the opening balance gives 9.6 times (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Tools of financial analysis — vertical analysis
questions.question: Which of the following is a tool of VERTICAL analysis?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Common-size statement
Why: Vertical analysis studies the relationship between items in the statements of ONE period, by expressing each item as a percentage of a base (revenue from operations, or total assets). The common-size statement does exactly this.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) compare figures across periods, which is horizontal analysis.
(D) A cash flow statement analyses changes in cash, not a vertical structure.
Key point: Horizontal = across years (comparative, trend); vertical = within one year (common-size).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — working capital turnover
questions.question: Revenue from operations is ₹12,00,000, current assets are ₹5,00,000 and current liabilities are ₹2,00,000. The working capital turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4 times
Formula: Working capital turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Working capital
Step 1: Working capital = ₹5,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000
Step 2: Ratio = ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹3,00,000 = 4 times
Common mistake: Dividing by current assets gives 2.4 times (A). Dividing by current liabilities gives 6 times (B). 2.5 (D) is the current ratio.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Graphs and charts for business data
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Chart)
(A) Column chart
(B) Line chart
(C) Pie chart
(D) Scatter (XY) chart

List-II (Best used to show)
(I) Comparison of values across categories
(II) Trend over a period of time
(III) Share of each part in a whole
(IV) Relationship between two numeric variables

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Column chart — compares values, e.g. sales of four branches → (I).
(B) Line chart — shows a trend, e.g. monthly profit over a year → (II).
(C) Pie chart — shows parts of a whole, e.g. the composition of expenses → (III).
(D) Scatter chart — shows the relationship between two variables, e.g. advertising spend versus sales → (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps column and line charts; (C) swaps line and pie charts; (D) swaps column and scatter charts.
Key point: Choose the chart according to the message the data must convey.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — asset bought during the year
questions.question: A machine is bought on 1 October 2025 for ₹1,20,000. It has a useful life of 5 years and no salvage value, and is depreciated on the straight-line method. The financial year ends on 31 March. In the depreciation schedule, the book value of the machine on 31 March 2027 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹84,000
Step 1: Annual depreciation = ₹1,20,000 ÷ 5 = ₹24,000
Step 2: 2025-26 (October to March, 6 months) = ₹24,000 × 6/12 = ₹12,000 → book value ₹1,08,000
Step 3: 2026-27 (full year) = ₹24,000 → book value ₹84,000
Common mistake: Charging two full years gives ₹72,000 (A). Charging only one full year gives ₹96,000 (B). Stopping after the first half-year gives ₹1,08,000 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Limitations of CAS
questions.question: Which of the following is a LIMITATION of a computerised accounting system?
options: B) High cost of installation and staff training
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) High cost of installation and staff training
Why: NCERT lists the limitations of CAS as the cost of installation (hardware and software), the cost of training, staff resistance, system failure, the inability to check unanticipated errors, and breaches of security.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are ADVANTAGES of CAS.
Key point: Limitations — cost, training, staff resistance, system failure, security risks.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Generating accounting information — SUMIF
questions.question: Cells A2:A6 contain the sale types Cash, Credit, Cash, Credit, Cash, and cells B2:B6 contain the amounts 500, 800, 300, 200, 700 respectively. The value returned by =SUMIF(A2:A6,"Cash",B2:B6) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1500
Step 1: Rows where column A = 'Cash': rows 2, 4 and 6
Step 2: The matching amounts in column B are 500, 300 and 700
Step 3: Sum = 500 + 300 + 700 = 1500
Common mistake: Adding all the amounts gives 2500 (A). Adding the credit sales gives 1000 (B). Counting the cash rows (=COUNTIF) gives 3 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Accounting Information System — components
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about an Accounting Information System (AIS):
(A) The people who use and operate the system are a component of AIS.
(B) Procedures and instructions are a component of AIS.
(C) Data relating to the organisation's business activities are a component of AIS.
(D) AIS deals only with non-financial data.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: An AIS is made up of people (users), procedures and instructions, data, software, IT infrastructure and internal controls. Together they collect, store and process accounting data into information for decision-makers.
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — AIS is mainly about FINANCIAL data (transactions), although it can also hold related non-financial data. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: AIS components — people, procedures, data, software, IT infrastructure, internal controls.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan repayment schedule — principal part of an EMI
questions.question: A loan of ₹3,00,000 at 12% p.a. is repaid in 3 equal annual instalments, each paid at the end of the year. The instalment works out to about ₹1,24,905. In the loan repayment schedule, the PRINCIPAL repaid in the first instalment (the value of =PPMT(12%,1,3,-300000)) is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹88,905
Given: Each equal instalment = interest on the outstanding balance + principal repaid.
Step 1: Interest for year 1 = 12% × ₹3,00,000 = ₹36,000
Step 2: Principal repaid = ₹1,24,905 − ₹36,000 = ₹88,905
Step 3: Balance after year 1 = ₹3,00,000 − ₹88,905 = ₹2,11,095 (the principal part grows each year as interest falls)
Common mistake: ₹1,00,000 (A) assumes equal principal of ₹3,00,000 ÷ 3. ₹1,24,905 (B) is the whole instalment (=PMT). ₹36,000 (D) is the interest part (=IPMT).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — functions
questions.question: Which spreadsheet function adds only those values that meet a given condition?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) SUMIF
Why: =SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) adds the cells in sum_range whose matching cells in range meet the criteria — for example, the total of only cash sales.
Why not the others:
(A) COUNT counts numeric cells.
(B) AVERAGE returns the mean.
(C) MAX returns the largest value.
Key point: SUMIF = conditional total; COUNTIF = conditional count.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — overtime with IF
questions.question: In a payroll sheet, overtime pay is calculated with =IF(D2>40,(D2-40)*E2*2,0), where D2 holds the hours worked in a week and E2 the hourly rate. If D2 = 46 and E2 = 200, the overtime pay is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2400
Step 1: Condition: 46 > 40 → TRUE
Step 2: Overtime hours = 46 − 40 = 6
Step 3: Overtime pay = 6 × 200 × 2 (double rate) = 2400
Common mistake: Forgetting the ×2 gives 1200 (A). Paying all the hours at the normal rate gives 46 × 200 = 9200 (C). Taking the FALSE branch gives 0 (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Codification — methods of coding
questions.question: Codes such as 'SAL' for Salary, 'RNT' for Rent and 'ADV' for Advertisement, which help users remember what the code stands for, are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mnemonic codes
Why: Mnemonic codes are made of letters (or letters and digits) that act as memory aids, so the code suggests the item it represents.
Why not the others:
(A) Sequential codes number items one after another (001, 002 …).
(B) Block codes assign ranges of numbers to groups (e.g. 1000–1999 for assets).
(C) Numeric codes use digits only, with no memory link.
Key point: NCERT's methods of codification are sequential, block and mnemonic codes.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — VLOOKUP
questions.question: In a payroll sheet, the formula =VLOOKUP(E2,$A$2:$C$10,3,FALSE) is used. This formula:
options: A) Adds all the values in the third column of A2:C10
B) Finds an exact match for E2 in the first column of A2:C10 and returns the value from the third column of that row
C) Returns the third smallest value in A2:C10
D) Counts how many cells in A2:C10 are equal to E2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Finds an exact match for E2 in the first column of A2:C10 and returns the value from the third column of that row
Why: VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, range_lookup) searches the FIRST column of the table for the lookup value. FALSE means an exact match. It then returns the value from the given column (3) of the same row — for example, fetching an employee's basic pay using his employee code.
Why not the others:
(A) describes SUM.
(C) describes SMALL.
(D) describes COUNTIF.
Key point: VLOOKUP = look up a key, return a related field.
